newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Too late to open Bulgarian police files - minister.
newsitem.headline: Too late to open Bulgarian police files - minister.

text.p: Interim Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev says it is too late to open Bulgaria's secret police files as the newly elected government proposes because he believes they have been subject to tampering since the end of one-party rule seven years ago.
Bonev, who is expected to retain his post in a post-election cabinet to be formed next month, told the daily newspaper Kontinent in an interview that he hoped the files would not be opened.
"I suspect that (the secret police files) have been destroyed selectively," he said.
"I don't know of any country which has opened its files seven years after the fall of a totalitarian regime. Maybe we have missed the right time, we should have done this in 1990."
The Union of Democratic Forces, which won last Saturday's parliamentary election, wants police files on members of parliament, cabinet ministers and supreme court judges to be opened.

Opening secret police files has been a controversial step even in what was East Germany, although made easier by the clean break the former communist state made with the past by unifying with the then West Germany and disbanding its own intelligence service.

In Bulgaria, security officials say that wholesale opening of the files could pose a risk to national security. Political surveillance has been abolished, but national security institutions continue to operate as in other countries.
The seven years since the end of one-party rule have given ample opportunity for files to be forged, substituted or destroyed.
Bulgaria's communist secret service, closely allied to the Soviet KGB, had a network of 100,000 agents and informers.

After a Grand National Assembly was formed in 1990 following the collapse of communism, a commission was set up to check on the past of its 400 members. Twenty-two of them were found to have cooperated with the security services.
Debate on what to do with the files has taken up a large amount of parliamentary time in the past seven years but the issue has never been resolved.

Several prominent UDF figures, including former leaders Filip Dimitrov and Petar Beron, have been accused of having cooperated with the security services, and the issue has even affected the Orthodox church.
Opponents of Patriarch Maxim, who was appointed during the communist era, enthroned their own patriarch, who was accused in turn by Maxim's followers of being an informer.
